title: Fallback lattice and SDK compactification — PRD draft
body:
Purpose: This doc proposes two interlocking product primitives to improve resiliency and developer ergonomics for the Hosted API streaming+tool surface: (1) a fallback lattice for coordinated, predictable automatic degradations across model, tool, region, and latency tiers; and (2) SDK compactification — a minimal handshake and microframe protocol intended for low-bandwidth/edge clients and simpler integration patterns.

Problem statement: Teams using the Hosted API want predictable behavior when capacity or tools fail, and a simple SDK that minimizes client complexity while preserving structured output guarantees. Current approaches attempt ad-hoc fallbacks (model -> smaller model -> retry) and heavyweight SDK handshakes that leak complexity (session sync, full tool schemas). Observed issues: surprising quality regressions, inconsistent tool semantics on fallback, inflated client state, and high integration effort for mobile/embedded apps.

Goals:
- Provide an explicit, pluggable fallback lattice that coordinates fallback decisions across axes (model, tool variant, region, latency tier) and surfaces deterministic behavior to clients and dashboards.
- Make streaming and tool-calling robust: partial results should be committable or resumable with clear developer-visible semantics.
- Reduce SDK surface area for low-footprint clients via compact microframes, progressive schema patches, and an idempotent commit token model.
- Maintain structured-output guarantees: schema negotiation, typed deltas, and tool-call confirmations survive fallbacks.

Non-goals:
- Replace full-featured SDKs for heavy-server clients. This is targeted at low-footprint, high-latency/unstable-network use cases and for teams that prioritize integration speed.
- Introduce new billing models — will use existing per-token/embedding billing.

Personas / Scenarios:
- Mobile app (edge) that streams user prompt, wants typed JSON steps, and may lose network mid-stream.
- Platform team embedding Hosted API as a microservice that must guarantee tool-call atomicity across model fallbacks.
- Developer experimenting with tool call graphs who needs deterministic dev-time behavior when retries happen.

Design overview — Fallback lattice (novelty):
- Lattice axes: model-fidelity, tool-fidelity, region, latency-tier. Each request has an ordered lattice path expressed in a compact policy blob (e.g., [hosted:high-fid, hosted:medium-fid] x [tool:primary, tool:readonly] x [region:closest, region:secondary] x [latency:fast, latency:best-effort]).
- Lattice semantics: a partial order (not a linear chain). Runtime reduces along lattice nodes according to constraints (SLO, cost, policy). Fallback is deterministic: given same lattice and runtime state, the resolved node will be identical.
- Coordinated fallback: on model fallback, the runtime consults lattice for compatible tool variants and schema capabilities. If a tool variant lacks capability, runtime either falls back tool-fidelity or responds with an explicit graceful-degradation frame.
- Observability: each lattice decision emits a deterministic event (lattice-path, chosen-node, reason). Console shows the active path and quality delta estimate.

Design overview — SDK compactification (novelty):
- Microframes: minimal JSONL events, each <= 2KB commonly (header-lite). Types: open, delta, tool-intent, tool-confirm, commit, resume, patch-schema, keepalive.
- Commit tokens: tentative frames are stamped with a commit token. Tools may return pre-commit judgments (e.g., confidence scores). When the runtime resolves a fallback, it returns final commit confirmation or a resume token for continuation.
- Schema patches: structured-output begins with an optional schema mask (lightweight), then diffs as the stream proceeds. Clients can opt into strict-mode (reject unknowns) or tolerant-mode (accept unknowns with tags).
- Offline-friendly resume: clients can reconnect with a resume token and microframe cursor. Resume token encodes chosen lattice node + commit tokens of uncommitted frames. This makes resume deterministic across fallbacks.

Tool-calling model refinements:
- Two-phase tool intent: clients send tool-intent microframe (idempotent). Runtime returns acceptance or mediated-rewrite (if tool not available on chosen node). If mediated-rewrite occurs, client receives a tool-proxy descriptor (synthetic call or read-only variant).
- Tool fidelity ladder: tool variants are typed with capability signatures. The lattice maps tool-fidelity entries to compatible models. If a lower-fidelity tool is chosen, runtime emits a fidelity-delta frame describing capability loss and expected output differences.

SDK ergonomics: developer-facing examples and quickstarts (sketch):
- Minimal JS streaming example (pseudocode in doc) shows microframe open -> streaming deltas -> tool-intent -> commit. Client code stays tiny: 2 handlers (onFrame, onReconnect) and a small retry/backoff.
- Native mobile patterns: use small persistent resume token store; opt into compressed frames for cellular.
- Migration: server-side adapters will translate existing full-session semantics into microframe patterns for backwards compatibility.

Examples (prose snippets):
- Failure case: model preemption mid-stream. Runtime resolves lattice -> chooses medium-fid model and readonly-tool variant; returns a lattice-change frame and a resume token. Client calls onReconnect with resume token; microframes replay uncommitted deltas; final commit acknowledged.

Telemetry & Success metrics:
- Decrease in customer-reported quality regressions during failover windows (target 40% reduction first 90 days).
- Median resume time for interrupted sessions under 1.2s for edge clients.
- SDK adoption: >30 teams integrate compact SDK in first 6 months.
- Observability signals: lattice-decision-rate, fidelity-delta-events, resume-success-rate, uncommitted-frame-leak-rate.

Operational considerations:
- Backwards compatibility: default lattice policy is conservative (prefer high-fid models) unless tenant opts-in. Existing full SDKs remain supported.
- Security: resume tokens are short-lived HMACed blobs; tool-intent frames do not leak secrets. Review with security and compliance required for private deployments.
- Costs: compact frames reduce network egress; however potential increases in small ticket retries must be monitored.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How to represent semantic quality delta estimates in a way that is actionable for customers? (Signal noise vs. usefulness.)
- Where to draw boundary for automatic mediated rewrites vs. returning an explicit error to devs?
- How to instrument fidelity-loss to avoid over-alerting?

Next steps / roadmap (proposed):
- M0 (3 weeks): implement lattice policy schema + simulator; define microframe wire format and JS reference.
- M1 (6 weeks): runtime lattice resolver + console events; beta of compact SDK for internal mobile teams.
- M2 (12 weeks): public beta, migrate one internal client (developer playground) to compact SDK, add schema-patch tooling in Optimize.

Appendix: quick checklist for implementation owners:
- Runtime: lattice resolver, fallback determinism tests, resume token HMAC.
- SDK: JS and iOS reference, small binary framing lib.
- Console: lattice visualization, fidelity-delta breadcrumbs.
- Observability: add dedicated metrics and trace tags.

Notes to reviewers: this is a sketch meant to provoke conversation about a more explicit and deterministic fallback model and a minimal SDK surface for low-footprint clients. Feedback request: prioritize (a) deterministic resume semantics vs (b) richer diagnostics in frames.

References: inline tickets and the streaming playbook.
